idiom_name: Ktor typed authentication with roles (withRoles + authenticateWith(roles = setOf(Role.Admin))); Spring Security @PreAuthorize works unchanged from Kotlin
implementation_notes: Ktor ships role-based authorization on top of its type-safe authentication: declare the role vocabulary as a type implementing AuthenticationRole (an enum is typical), extend a base scheme with withRoles { principal -> roleService.resolveRoles(principal.id) }, and require roles per route with authenticateWith(roleScheme, roles = setOf(Role.Admin)) - a caller lacking a required role gets 403 through the configurable onForbidden handler, and the resolved roles are visible as call.principal.roles only inside a role-aware scheme. The role set therefore comes from a server-side resolver (a database read, cached per request), not from the token. On the Spring stack the same JVM primitives as Java apply verbatim from Kotlin - @EnableMethodSecurity with @PreAuthorize("hasRole('PAUSER')") on a service method and a RoleHierarchy bean - so the choice is the host framework, not the language. Either way the enforcement seam is the route or bean boundary and deny-by-default is a configuration (a fallback/any-request rule), not a built-in default.
pitfalls: Roles are only exposed on a role-aware scheme; call.principal.roles from a plain authenticateWith route is empty or fails, so wrap the route in the withRoles scheme.
Resolving roles from the database on every request adds a lookup to the hot path; cache the resolution per request or session and invalidate on assignment change.
An authenticateWith block protects only the routes inside it - a sibling route declared outside is anonymous; nest protected routes under one root or add a deny fallback.
With Spring, @PreAuthorize on a Kotlin extension or a private method is not proxied and never runs; keep annotated methods open and on the bean boundary.
Taking roles from JWT claims instead of the resolver keeps a revoked role alive until the token expires.
